system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 2 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A 68-year-old male with a history of non-ischemic cardiomyopathy (LVEF 25%), ICD, chronic kidney disease, and a right humeral fracture was admitted for acute shortness of breath worsening when lying flat, consistent with fluid overload from heart failure exacerbation. Evaluation showed minimal pulmonary edema on chest X-ray, elevated BNP, and no acute ischemia. He was treated with IV furosemide and transitioned to increased oral torsemide. His diabetes was managed with insulin during admission due to elevated blood glucose, and he was restarted on glipizide at discharge. Insomnia and depression were addressed with continuation of imipramine and perphenazine, and initiation of mirtazapine. Subtherapeutic INR led to warfarin dose increase. He improved clinically, with resolution of pulmonary crackles and stable vital signs, and was discharged home with medication adjustments and follow-up plans.
problems: Acute on chronic systolic heart failure
Diabetes mellitus without mention of complication, type II or unspecified type, not stated as uncontrolled
Closed fracture of surgical neck of humerus

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, Mr. Smith. I'm Dr. Lee, one of the hospitalists. I understand you've been having trouble breathing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, doctor. It’s been getting worse over the last two days. I can’t lie flat anymore—I need three pillows now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any chest pain, fever, or cough?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, none of that. But I’ve gained about 8 pounds recently. I think I ate a bit more salt than usual.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That could definitely be part of it. We’ve reviewed your chest X-ray and labs. The X-ray shows some fluid in your lungs—mild pulmonary edema—which fits with a heart failure flare-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh. Like last time? I’ve had this before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, very similar. Your BNP level is elevated, which confirms fluid overload. But good news—no signs of infection or heart attack.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what’s the plan?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll give you IV diuretics—furosemide—to help your body get rid of the extra fluid. You already got some in the ER and we’ll continue that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Will I be here long?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Likely a couple of days. We want to make sure your breathing improves and your oxygen levels stay stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright. My blood pressure and sugar—should I worry?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood pressure is okay. Your glucose was a bit high—201—but we’re monitoring it. We’ll keep you on insulin for now and restart your glipizide later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my heart medicine? I take warfarin, amiodarone, metoprolol…

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re continuing all your heart meds. Amiodarone, metoprolol, spironolactone—all staying the same.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better, I think. I can breathe easier. Still a little short of breath when I walk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good progress. You’ve lost over a liter of fluid already. We’re switching from IV furosemide to IV torsemide—same goal, just different med.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that stronger?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It lasts longer in your system. You’ve responded well so far—total diuresis over 3 liters now. Your oxygen is 95% on two liters, which is much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. What about my kidney numbers? They usually go up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your creatinine is 1.7, which is a bit higher than your baseline of 1.3. That’s expected with diuresis and heart failure. We’re watching it closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my INR? I’m on warfarin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your INR came back at 1.4, which is a little low. We gave you an extra 4mg dose yesterday to bring it up. Please keep your next INR appointment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I will. And my depression meds—I take imipramine and perphenazine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’ve been taking those. We’re continuing both. Mirtazapine at night too, for sleep and appetite.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve been sleeping better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow morning if things keep improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep taking your torsemide daily. We’re not changing your dose now, but follow up with cardiology—they may adjust it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I thought I was supposed to take it twice a day sometimes?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Ah, yes. Your discharge instructions say: take one tablet twice a day on days you feel more short of breath or notice swelling, then go back to once daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And salt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Very important—low-salt diet. And weigh yourself every morning. Call your doctor if you gain more than 3 pounds in a day or two.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do that. And my omeprazole for reflux?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re cutting it to 20mg twice a day. You were on 40mg, but this should still control your symptoms and be safer for your kidneys.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Most are the same. We’re adjusting metoprolol to 75mg total daily, split into three doses for smoother control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright. I think I’ve got it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared to go home. Your breathing is much better, and your oxygen is over 93% walking around.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a few reminders: keep up with your low-salt diet, daily weights, and follow up with cardiology and your primary doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the INR check?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, please get that done as scheduled. We gave you an extra warfarin dose to help, but we need to make sure it’s in the right range.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And if I start feeling short of breath again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call your doctor. If it’s severe, don’t wait—go to the ER. But I think you’re on the right track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate all the help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—my diabetes. Should I check my sugar more often?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, check it twice a day. We’ve restarted your glipizide. If your sugars stay high, let your doctor know.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And keep taking your aspirin, statin, and all the other meds as listed in your discharge instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll review them when I get home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Nurse will go over everything one more time before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks again, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Stay well.

summary.summary_paragraph: A 68-year-old male with a history of non-ischemic cardiomyopathy (LVEF 25%), ICD, chronic kidney disease, and diabetes was admitted for acute shortness of breath and orthopnea worsened by recent salt intake. Evaluation revealed interstitial pulmonary edema on chest X-ray, elevated BNP, and no acute ischemia. He was treated with IV furosemide and torsemide, achieving over 3 liters of diuresis and symptomatic improvement. His oxygen saturation stabilized above 93% on room air. Diabetes was managed with insulin during admission, and oral glipizide was resumed at discharge. Warfarin was continued, though INR remained subtherapeutic at 1.4, prompting an additional dose and emphasis on follow-up monitoring. He was discharged home with instructions to maintain a low-salt diet, monitor daily weights, and follow up with cardiology and primary care.
